A box of five civilian emergency ration bars, each wrapped in heavy foil with a printed date. One box restores a large amount of hunger, enough to carry a person through a day of work. The bars are dense and dry and keep for years. This box is one of the last in the district.

A single emergency ration bar in foil, dense and sweet, dated three years ago. It restores a large amount of hunger for its weight and keeps a scavenger moving through a long day. The foil is creased at the corners from being carried. Ration bars are the most trusted paper money there is.

A can of fish in oil, heavy in the hand and sealed tight. It restores a full day's worth of hunger and the oil holds the flavor through the years. Protein is the hardest thing to find in the wasteland, which is why the can trades high. The label is printed in a language no one reads anymore.

A can of beans in thin sauce, plain and heavy. It restores a large amount of hunger and goes further stretched into a pot of rice. The can has no label, just a paper date stamped on the lid. Beans are what most shelters actually live on.

A jar of jam preserves, dark and thick and heavy with sugar. It restores some hunger and gives a strong lift, the taste of fruit and sweetness together. The jar is a reused pickle jar with a handwritten label. Sugar is remembered in the wasteland better than most things.

A prepared breakfast bowl: porridge or oats, warm and plain, packed for eating on the move. It restores a solid amount of hunger and a little thirst. The bowl is stackable and the lid snaps shut. It tastes of the pot it came from, which is to say it tastes of nothing much.

A prepared dinner bowl, hot and heavy with gravy, meat, or what passes for it. It restores the most hunger of the prepared meals and gives a strong lift to the person who eats it. The lid is sealed so it can be carried home. It is the closest thing to a good dinner in the wasteland.

A prepared oat breakfast with something sweet folded in, dried fruit or honey when the season was good. It restores a large amount of hunger and gives a real lift. The portions are measured and even. It is the breakfast worth getting up for, and people queue for it.

A ceramic water filter element, the candle type for a gravity filter system. It takes silt, grit, and most of what makes runoff dangerous out of the water, and it holds eighty units of use before the pores clog. A clean candle is worth more than gold in a dry district. This one is still sealed in its wrap.

A manual can opener with a turning handle and a gear that walks itself around the rim. It opens every can in the larder and holds full condition if it is dried after use. The handle is worn smooth at the grip. The ones with the gear are the ones people keep.

A crude can opener: a lever and a cutting edge, or a blade ground into a spike. It opens a can roughly, leaving jagged edges that cut fingers when you hurry. It holds only twenty units of use before it dulls, but it is cheap and easy to replace. Every shop has a bucket of them.

A vacuum flask with a steel shell and a cup that doubles as the lid. It keeps water hot through a night shift or cold through a summer walk, a quiet tool with no moving parts. Half a kilo carried against the chest. The one that never leaked was worth keeping out of any trade.

Small pressed pills of dried herbs, dark and slightly bitter. They ease a worn body a little, restoring a small amount of health for a person who is run down. They are made by hand in batches and sold by the bottle. The recipe is a trade secret in the district that makes them.

A cloth bandage with a poultice of crushed herbs pressed into the pad. It cleans a wound and restores a small amount of health while it is worn. The cloth is boiled before it is rolled. It is the first thing a shelter medic reaches for when the real supplies run out.

A clean rolled bandage of gauze, tight and white at the center. It dresses a wound and restores a fair amount of health, better than cloth strips, and it keeps if it stays dry. Medical supplies this clean are worth carrying out of any raid, even when the rest of the shelf is picked clean.

A proper medical kit: bandages, antiseptic, tape, scissors, and a sheet of instructions folded in the lid. It restores a large amount of health in one go and is the single most reliable patch in most shelters. One kit weighs over a kilo and is treated like a family member. It came from a clinic that did not survive.

A box of six adhesive bandages, each in its own paper sleeve. They cover small cuts and scrapes and restore a small amount of health. The box is thin and fits in a pocket. Children's bandages with cartoons on them are worth more than plain ones, which says something about the wasteland.

A one liter bottle of antiseptic solution, clear and sealed. It cleans a wound before dressing, and a wound cleaned first heals better than one that is not. A liter lasts a long time if it is measured out. The bottle is heavy and travels poorly, so it stays in the shelter.

A sealed sterile dressing, vacuum packed, the kind that keeps for years. It restores a good amount of health and does not infect the wound it covers. The pack is crinkled from being carried in a jacket. It is the standard dressing in the medkit and the first thing medics hoard.

Prescription opioid tablets, small and bitter, in a pharmacy bottle. They dull pain and restore a fair amount of health, and they give a dangerous kind of lift on top. People hoard them and watch their own dosage. The bottle is half full, which means someone rationed it carefully.

A box of ten sealed alcohol wipes, each in its own foil pouch. They clean skin before an injection or a dressing and take the worst of the dirt off a wound. A full box holds its value because the seal is intact. They smell of the only clean thing left in the world.

A bottle of twenty antibiotic tablets, white and scored down the middle. A course restores a large amount of health, and finishing the course matters as much as starting it. The bottle is worth more than gold to a shelter with a fever in it. The prescription label has a name scratched out.

An auto-injector pen in a plastic case, one dose, one use. It restores a large amount of health fast and can hold a body together until help or a bed arrives. It was meant for allergic shock and is used for everything worse. People who carry one check the case twice a week.

A thermometer, glass with a printed scale or digital with a dead screen. It tells a fever from the cold and decides who rests and who works. It weighs nothing and trades small. The glass ones are the ones that still work; the mercury never lies.

Blunt-tipped surgical scissors with a curve at the jaw. They cut bandages and clothing without touching the skin underneath, which is the whole trick. They hold eighty units of wear before the joint loosens. A medic without a good pair of scissors works with a knife, and it shows.

A bottle of ten potassium iodide tablets, sealed in foil and dated. Taken before exposure, they saturate the thyroid so inhaled iodine cannot lodge there. Ten tablets is a ten day course, one a day, and the bottle should be counted out carefully. It is the one tablet that decides who sickens later.

A pencil shaped dosimeter on a spring clip, with a scale marked in the window. It measures the dose already taken, not the dose coming, and that is the useful part. It holds full condition and clips to a collar or a pocket. The scale on this one has been read out loud every night for a month.

A half face respirator with a rubber seal and a lens, made to take screw-in filters. It adds one point of rad protection while it is worn on the face, and the filters are sold separately. The seal holds eighty units of wear before the rubber hardens. In cold air the lens fogs and you breathe through the gap at the nose.

A box of five sealed respirator filter cartridges, each in foil. When the mask starts to taste of metal, one of these goes in. The box keeps them dry and clean. Filters are the difference between a mask that works and a mask that is just a weight.

A single respirator filter cartridge, sealed in foil with a date on the edge. It slots into the mask and takes the worst of the fallout out of the air a person breathes. One cartridge at a time, carried in a pocket so it stays clean. The foil is intact, which is the whole value.

Sealed plastic goggles with a foam edge and an adjustable strap. They keep ash out of the eyes on a windy day and dust out of a working face. They hold sixty units of wear before the strap or the seal goes. The lens scratches but the eyes behind it stay clean.

Thick rubber gloves that reach past the wrist. They let a person handle contaminated things without the skin taking the dose, and they are the cheapest insurance on the shelf. They hold forty units of wear before the rubber cracks at the cuff. Dry them inside out and they last.

A box of five bars of decontamination soap, beige and almost scentless. Washing with it lifts surface contamination off the skin before it turns into dose. One bar lasts a long time if the wash is done properly; order matters, soap first, rinse after. The box is kept near the entry of every careful shelter.

A box of five heavy plastic bags, thicker than a liner bag and printed with a warning. Contaminated clothing, filters, and gloves go in one, sealed, marked, and set aside. It stops the dose from walking through the shelter on a coat. The bags are cheap; the lesson that made them necessary was not.

A folding military shovel with a sharpened edge and a locking hinge. It digs a latrine, a trench, a grave, and cuts roots when the handle is reversed. It holds a hundred and forty units of wear, the most of any digging tool in the shelter. The paint is chipped to bare steel at the blade.

A short handled hatchet with a leather sheath and a wedge shaped head. It splits kindling, opens a stubborn door, and cuts its way out of a bad situation. It holds a hundred and twenty units of wear before the handle needs binding. The head is stamped with a date and an inspection mark.

A full length fire axe with a fiberglass shaft and a red painted head. It was built to break through doors, walls, and roof beams, and it still does all three. It holds a hundred and forty units of wear and weighs nearly three kilos behind the swing. It came off a truck that stopped answering calls.

Slip joint pliers with a wire cutter at the hinge. They grip, crimp, and pull what fingers cannot, and the cutter handles the thin wire that binds everything. They hold ninety units of wear before the jaws rock. A pair that fits a hand is kept close and loaned out only to friends.

A tin of ten needles, spools of thread, and a thimble, laid in a paper tray. Clothing and bags outlast the war only if they are mended, and this is what mends them. The kit holds full condition and the needles are oiled against rust. The thimble is dented, which means it was used.

A handheld flashlight with an anodized body and a rubber tail switch. It takes AA batteries, sold separately, and throws a clean beam across a room. It holds eighty units of wear before the switch or the lens gives. The batteries come out when it goes on the shelf, so the contacts stay bright.

A heavier flashlight with a metal bezel and a solid switch, made to be dropped. It takes the same batteries but holds a hundred and twenty units of wear. The beam is wide and steady. Soldiers carried these once; now the ones that still work are worth a small fortune in trade.

A stack of matchboxes, strike anywhere heads, wrapped to keep the damp out. One match lights a stove, a candle, or a smoke, and a box stretches a long way if the strikes are counted. The cardboard is soft from humidity. The flint strip on the side is still good.

A disposable lighter with most of its gas left, the flame low and blue. It lights a stove, a candle, or a smoke and sparks on the first try or the third. It weighs nothing and trades a little. The one that sparks first time is worth keeping in a pocket and out of the wind.

A twelve volt lead acid car battery, heavy as a block of the floor. It stores what the solar panels make during the day and pays it back at night, running the radio, the lights, and the workshop. It is not delicate but it is heavy at twelve kilos. Two of them in rotation keep a shelter going.

A rechargeable battery in a standard size, ready to take a charge from a panel or a generator. It cycles again and again while the single use cells run dry. It holds its charge longer if it is not left in the cold. A drawer of these is a small power station.

A pack of ten AA batteries, sealed in the original cardboard. They power radios, flashlights, and dosimeters, and they are gone for good once they are used. The pack is dated and still sealed. People count their batteries the way they count their bullets.

An AM and FM radio with a crank handle folded into the side. Thirty seconds of winding buys a few minutes of listening, no batteries, no grid, no argument. It holds full condition and sits in the center of the shelter. The voice on the broadcast is what people gather around.

A small folding solar panel with canvas edges and a cable. On a clear day it puts a charge into a battery, enough to keep the essentials alive. It is light enough to carry and tough enough to sit on the roof. The cells are scratched but they still answer to the sun.

A full sized rigid solar panel in a metal frame, meant for a roof. It feeds steady power through the day and keeps a shelter's batteries honest. It weighs six kilos and mounts flat, cleaned of ash every few days. The frame was welded once and has held since.

A petrol generator, twenty five kilos of cast iron, coil, and crank. It runs the workshop, the lights, and the charges through the worst weeks, as long as fuel can be found. It holds full condition and starts on the second pull when it is warm. The sound of it running brings people to the door.

A brass kerosene lantern with a glass chimney and a wick wheel. It gives warm light that does not need batteries or a grid, just oil and a lit match. It holds ninety units of wear before the pump or the chimney goes. It hangs by the door so it is never lost in the dark.

A ten liter jerrycan of jet fuel, sealed and stamped with the grade. It burns hot and clean in generators and stoves, better than any pump grade found since. It weighs nine kilos full. The can was tapped from a depot before the pumps ran dry, and the seal has never been broken.

A heavy winter coat, padded and hooded, worn at the cuffs and mended at the elbow. It keeps the nuclear winter off a body working outdoors, and it holds eighty units of wear before the fill packs down. It is the first thing checked out of the common stores when the temperature drops. It was somebody's, once.

Steel toe work boots, resoled twice, laces replaced with cord. They hold a hundred units of wear and take the daily weight of walking the ash. The soles are stitched, which is why they still hold. Good boots are the difference between working and watching.

A thick wool blanket, gray, with a moth hole mended in the corner. It gives a real lift to whoever sleeps under it, and sleep under wool is better than sleep without. It holds its warmth even damp. The blanket outlived its first owner and will outlive its second.

A roll of foam with canvas straps, the kind that sleeps one person off the floor. It rolls small and rides on a pack frame. It is not a bed, but it is not the ground either. The foam is dense where it is sat on and still springs back.

A bed on a wooden frame, stuffed with wool and covered in a heavy tick. It sleeps one person properly, off the floor, out of the draft. It weighs eight kilos of wood and wool and takes a corner of the shelter. It is the most expensive comfort most people own.

A bed with a heating element built under the sleeping surface and a plug that reaches the power line. It heats the sleeping space without an open flame in the room, which matters in a wooden shelter. It weighs twelve kilos and trades for the price of a good tool. Cold nights are measured against it.

Knitted wool gloves, wet and dried stiff once, now shaped to the hands. They hold fifty units of wear and keep fingers working in the cold, which is worth more than they cost. The thumbs are reinforced with leather patches. A person without gloves works half a day before giving up.

A photograph in a cracked frame: three people standing in front of a car, one hand raised to wave. It gives a strong lift to whoever keeps it, a steady five on the morale scale. It trades cheap and is traded rarely. The glass is taped at the corner where it cracked.

A cassette tape with handwriting on the label: a name, a date, a list of songs. It gives a real lift when a player and batteries can be found. The tape has been rewound so many times the clear leader is worn. It is the only record of a voice that is gone.

A sealed envelope with an official stamp and a red string binding. The contents are someone's business and not the holder's. It has no trade value and no use, which means someone wants it and someone else wants it gone. The seal is unbroken. It was entrusted to the wrong person on purpose.

A cut diamond in a worn velvet box, the clasp loose. It weighs almost nothing and carries the highest trade value of the stones, worth a stack of food to the right trader. It was an engagement stone once, or an inheritance. The box is kept because the stone needs somewhere to live.

A cut ruby, dark red, in a plain box. It trades high, a little under the diamond, and buys medicine or fuel when the right buyer comes. Stones hold value because they do not spoil and do not need feeding. It came out of a jewelry case that was buried for two years.

A cut sapphire, deep blue, the color of old ink. It trades steadily and keeps its value while food rots. The stone weighs nothing and fits in a sealed pocket. It was meant for a ring that was never made. Some traders keep stones for the day the money comes back.

A piece of amber with an insect sealed inside, polished smooth. It trades at a fraction of the gemstones but moves faster, because it looks like nothing else on a counter. It was a pendant once. The insect inside has been dead longer than anyone alive.

A 9x19 service pistol with a steel frame and a double stacked grip, a little over a kilo. It holds a hundred and twenty units of wear and has outlived its maker's company. The caliber is the point: 9x19 is the common round, and a pistol chambered for it is easier to feed than one that is not.

A 9x19 service pistol with an open slide and a steel frame, one point one five kilos. It holds a hundred and twenty units of wear. Soldiers carried these once, and the ones that survived the exchange now trade hands in shelters. It shoots flat and feeds the common 9x19 round.

A 9x19 pistol with a polymer frame, light at under a kilo. It holds a hundred and twenty units of wear and carries easy on a belt. The sights are plain and the grip is smooth. It was a modern piece once and is still a good one, chambered for the round everyone has.

A letter dated before the exchange, folded and unfolded many times along the same creases. It gives a small lift to whoever reads it, a fraction of what a photograph does. It trades for almost nothing and is kept for reasons that have nothing to do with trade. The ink is still sharp.

A charcoal sketch on gray paper: a house with a fence, a tree, a line of washing. It gives a real lift to whoever keeps it and trades for almost nothing, which is how it ended up kept. Someone drew their home from memory. The paper is smudged at the bottom from being handled.

Leather frame goggles with dark lenses and an elastic strap. They cut the glare off snow and ash both, and they give a small lift while worn, comfort against the white. They hold only thirty units of wear before the strap or the stitching goes. They were made for the mountains, not the ash, but they work.

A compact .380 ACP pistol, light at six tenths of a kilo, small enough for a coat pocket. It holds a hundred units of wear and goes where it is told. The caliber is light but the gun is honest, and a small pistol that works beats a big one that stays home.

A .380 ACP pistol with a polymer frame, seven tenths of a kilo. It holds a hundred and ten units of wear and is simpler to take apart than most, which matters when the manual is gone. The slide runs smooth. It was a modern police piece once.

A 7.62x25 service pistol with a roller locked action and a steel frame, under a kilo. It holds a hundred and fifteen units of wear. The cartridge is flat shooting and old, and the gun is built heavier than it needs to be. It was made to be used hard and it still accepts it.

A 7.62x25 pistol, stamped steel, just under nine tenths of a kilo. It holds a hundred and ten units of wear. It is a copy of a service design, made in numbers that mean spares can be found. The finish is worn at the edges, which is the honest kind of wear.

A 7.62x25 service pistol, nine tenths of a kilo, with a steel frame and fixed sights. It holds a hundred and fifteen units of wear. It was built in a factory that no longer exists, for a military that no longer exists, and it still feeds and fires. The bluing is rubbed at the holster line.

A .45 ACP submachine gun with a wooden stock and heavy steel, four point eight kilos of it. It holds a hundred and forty units of wear. The design is older than everyone alive and still goes to work when the trigger is pulled. It was built for a war that happened before, and it never learned to stop.

A .45 ACP submachine gun with a polymer receiver and a folding stock, two point three kilos. It holds a hundred and thirty units of wear. It was a police piece once, clean and modern, and it is easier to carry than anything else in its class. It runs dry and clean and asks little back.

A .45 ACP submachine gun with an unusual angled action that keeps the muzzle flat through a burst. It weighs two point seven kilos and holds a hundred and thirty five units of wear. It was an expensive experiment once and is now just a tool that works. The action is odd to take apart, but it feeds the common .45 round.

A compact .45 ACP pistol in a folding package, two point one kilos. It holds a hundred and twenty five units of wear. It is built like a rifle and sized like a pistol, which is why it trades so high. It folds small for the bag and comes out ready when the bag opens.

Compact blowback submachine gun chambered in .45 ACP. At 2.5 kg it balances light enough for long carries, and the 140 durability reads in the frame's settled feel, the bolt group still tight after years of handling. .45 rounds keep pushing through doors and heavy coats where smaller calibers stop. Traders price it at 185 because the caliber is still made somewhere and the gun refuses to die. Most survivors keep one folded in a pack, a weight they notice only when it is gone.

Selective-fire submachine gun in 9x21, built around a double-column magazine feed that some armorers still talk about. At 2.9 kg it is heavier than it looks, and 130 durability means the plastic frame shows cracks before the steel does. The 9x21 round is flatter and harder than common 9x19, which matters when you shoot through a car door. Traders move it at 155 when the magazines come with it, and they always ask for the mags first.

The smallest of the Uzi line, stamped steel folded around a 2 kg frame that disappears under a coat. 120 durability is honest: it was built to be carried often and fired rarely. In 9x21 it throws a flat, fast round, and the open bolt means it will fire when it is cold, dirty, or wet, which is all that matters after three winters of ash. A 150 trade value with no paperwork and a story nobody asks about.

Polymer submachine gun chambered in 9x21, the folding stock and rail still straight on the 135-point frame. The trigger is long but the gun shoots flat, and the ambidextrous controls were a luxury once, now just the difference between a working hand and a numb one. At 2.5 kg it rides on a sling for a whole scavenging day without complaint. Worth 170 to anyone who needs something they can shoot one-handed while carrying a crate.

Early submachine gun in 7.65x21, all machined steel and 4.2 kg of it. The 145 durability is earned by thick receiver walls; these were made when guns were overbuilt because steel was cheap and war was anticipated. The caliber is thin by modern standards, but it feeds reliably and the gun simply will not stop working, which is why it still turns up in cellars. Traders take it at 140, mostly for the receiver as a donor for scrap and spare parts.

Brass-fitted submachine gun in 7.65x21, milled like a tool rather than stamped like a wartime expedient. 4.1 kg, 150 durability, and a wood stock that has outlived two owners, maybe three. It fires from a closed bolt, which makes it more accurate than most of its age, and the caliber is mild enough that even a tired shooter keeps the sights on target. It changes hands for 145, usually from an old man who needs food more than he needs the gun.

Semi-automatic 12 gauge with an inertia system that does not care about temperature, pressure, or how badly you are shaking. At 3.8 kg and 140 durability it is a working gun, the kind that gets cleaned by firelight and still cycles. Five shells of 12 gauge settle arguments at doorways faster than anything else you can carry one-handed. Worth 180 because it is the last word in shotguns that people actually trade, not the ones they pray over.

Gas-operated semi-automatic 12 gauge, 3.6 kg of familiar steel and walnut. The 130 durability reflects the years: these were hunting guns before the exchange, carried on shoulders through cornfields, not through ruins. It cycles soft loads cleanly, which matters when you reload with whatever shells you find. Traders price it at 150. A dead man's shotgun bought with a can of fuel and a promise.

Long-recoil semi-automatic 16 gauge, the barrel's recoil stroke still slick at 135 durability. 3.3 kg, and the humpback receiver dates it as a gun made to be handed down. The 16 gauge round is lighter than 12, which means less reach but a steadier swing for smaller shooters, and the shells are scarcer now, traded shell by shell. It sells for 140, and buyers check the serial number the way they check a person's hands.

Light semi-automatic 16 gauge at 2.8 kg, inertia-driven, with a receiver that shows 125 durability of honest wear. It carries all day on a walk between bunkers and comes up quick when something moves in the ash. The 16 gauge kick is mild enough for a teenager to learn on, and there are worse inheritances. Valued at 135, less than a 12 gauge, which says more about the ammo than about the gun.

Gas-impingement carbine in 5.56x45, 2.9 kg with the collapsing stock collapsed. 140 durability on the bolt and carrier means it was maintained, not just carried. The platform is common enough that parts trade like currency and armorers can fix one in their sleep, which is worth more than any single feature. At 190 it is the baseline rifle of the region: half the scavenged guns on the wall are this or something that copies it.

Short-stroke piston carbine in 5.56x45, 3.5 kg of rifle that runs cleaner than the gas-impingement guns because the piston keeps carbon out of the bolt. 150 durability and the finish still holds. It fires when it is cold, wet, and caked with ash, and the cold is the point: nuclear winter jams lesser guns with condensed moisture. At 220 it is one of the most expensive rifles a trader will put on the table.

Carbine in 5.56x45, 3.3 kg with the polymer lower that shrugs off cold. 145 durability, and the rails still hold zero after the mounts were dropped on concrete twice. The folding stock shortens it for tunnels, and the gas block can be tuned for suppressed fire, which matters more every year as noise gets answered faster. Traders ask 210 and rarely come down, because the gun is worth exactly that in meat and medicine.

Bullpup rifle in 5.56x45 with the integral optic that survived when cheaper scopes fogged. 3.6 kg of the weight sits over the shoulder, so the barrel stays up longer on a watch. 140 durability; the plastic stock is cold against a cheek but never rusts. A long rifle the length of a carbine, which is what you want in a bunker hallway. Worth 200, and the optic alone is why.

Rifle in 7.62x39, 4.3 kg of weapon that has crossed every border in the region at least twice. 160 durability means it has been dropped, buried, and cleaned with motor oil, and it still cycles. The 7.62x39 round punches through walls and winter coats. At 175 it is cheap for what it is, but the price reflects supply, not respect: there are more of these than there are people left to carry them.

AR-pattern rifle converted to 7.62x39, 3.2 kg with the curved magazine that feeds the tapered round without a jam. 135 durability; the conversion is recent enough that the parkerization still smells when it gets warm. It gives an AR shooter the reach of an AK round with controls they already know. Worth 185, but the magazines are the real asset, and sellers count them separately.

Bipod-fed light machine gun in 5.45x39, 4.7 kg of sustained fire built around a heavy barrel. 150 durability; the barrel is thick enough for long bursts without walking the heat into the stock. The 5.45 round is light to carry, so a belt means more minutes of fire than an equal weight of anything bigger. Worth 195, and the bipod has held up a thousand sightlines.

Shortened carbine in 5.45x39, 2.7 kg of compact rifle that folds short enough for a duffel. 135 durability, and the fireball from the short barrel announces you from half a block, but in tight rooms nobody cares. The 5.45 round is flat and light, and the gun rides in a vehicle like it was made for it. Worth 170, most often carried by people who plan to be close.

Battle rifle in 7.62x51, 4.3 kg of machined steel that has been called many things and is simply heavy, reliable, and true. 145 durability; the gas system can be dialed for reduced loads, which matters when you run whatever ammunition you find. The 7.62x51 round reaches and hits like nothing lighter. At 230 it is the most expensive of the old battle rifles, and the price has never once been argued.

Roller-delayed battle rifle in 7.62x51, 4.4 kg with the fluted chamber that ejects even in mud. 150 durability; these were built for armies that expected to keep them for decades. The roller lock makes the action forgiving of dirty ammunition, and the caliber does the rest. Worth 225, and the stamped receiver has a serial number, a unit mark, and a long silence around where it came from.

Integrally suppressed carbine in .300 BLK, 2.1 kg and quiet enough that the bolt cycling is the loudest part. 130 durability on the suppressor means the baffles are wearing thin, and it sounds like it. The round is subsonic, which drops the reach but keeps the gun under a shout in close cover. At 240 it is a specialist's rifle, and sellers usually take payment in ammunition it can actually fire.

Short-stroke piston carbine in .300 BLK with a short barrel folded down to a 2.6 kg package that fits in a daypack. 140 durability; the folding stock and telescoping rail are the most expensive parts of the gun, and they show it. It loses velocity out of the short barrel, so the range is honest: close, quiet, final. Worth 250 because small guns that still shoot accurately are the hardest kind to find.

Gas-piston PDW carbine in .300 BLK, 2.5 kg with a stock that collapses around the receiver like a skeleton. 135 durability; the rail and the bolts are all aircraft-grade and the gun shows no rust, which is remarkable after three years of ash. It carries subsonic loads cleanly with the suppressor on. Worth 235, usually bought by people who measure a doorframe with their rifle before they enter it.

Bullpup personal defense weapon in 5.7x28, 2.6 kg with the magazine lying flat along the top of the receiver. 140 durability; the polymer body was built for vehicle crews who dropped it between seats and forgot it. The 5.7 round is small, flat, and light, and it defeats light armor at close range, which is exactly the argument it was designed to make. Worth 220, and the ammo is the bottleneck, not the gun.

Take-down carbine in 5.7x28, 2.7 kg that splits into two pieces for a pack. 130 durability; the barrel collar still locks tight, which is the part that usually gives out. The 5.7 round is light to carry, so a hundred rounds feel like thirty. It shares ammunition with the PDWs, which is convenient when your group carries both. Worth 180 to people who plan to walk far and shoot little.

Personal defense weapon in 4.6x30 at 1.9 kg, the lightest gun that still counts as a firearm in most traders' scales. 135 durability; the polymer lower and folding grip make it nearly pocketable under a coat. The 4.6x30 round is a needle that defeats vests at close range. Worth 230, and a full magazine is worth more than the gun to the people who have both.

AR-pattern PDW in 4.6x30, 2.4 kg with a compact gas system that keeps the bolt clean. 130 durability; it feeds the small, sharp round without the jams that plague other 4.6 conversions. The round is light enough to carry two hundred without noticing, flat enough to hold a line. Worth 210, usually traded between armorers who agree on the ammunition, because nobody else stocks it.

Machined PDW in 4.6x30, 2.2 kg, all billet aluminum with a handguard that wraps the barrel like a glove. 130 durability and no plastic anywhere, which is why it still looks new. It is a small gun that shoots like a rifle at close range, and the 4.6x30 round keeps its speed out of a short barrel. Worth 215; a specialized gun for a specialized round, and both are hard to find.

Bolt-action rifle in 7.62x54R, 4.0 kg of wood, steel, and history. 160 durability: it was built before the exchange, before the last war, and it will be functional after whoever carries it now is gone. The action is simple enough to fix with a file, and the round reaches across a field. Worth 160, and every family in the region has a story attached to one of these.

Semi-automatic marksman rifle in 7.62x54R, 4.3 kg with a gas piston tuned for quick aimed fire. 145 durability; the wood stock is dinged but the barrel is straight, which is all that counts. It shares ammunition with the bolt guns, so a marksman and a farmer can feed one rifle from one crate. Worth 260, and the scope has a number on it that nobody asks about.

Dragunov-pattern semi-automatic rifle in 7.62x54R, 4.2 kg built on an enlarged receiver. 140 durability; the steel is plain but the action is honest, and it will shoot as long as there is ammunition. It is a marksman's rifle that costs less than the imports, which is why it shows up in the hands of people who cannot afford better. Worth 240, and the magazines are getting rare.

Precision bolt rifle in .338 Lapua, 5.7 kg with the chassis machined around the action like a cast. 150 durability; the barrel is free-floated and the trigger breaks like a glass rod. The .338 round reaches past a kilometer and drops through wind that pushes smaller bullets off. Worth 320, and the scope on top costs more than most people's rifles.

Match-grade bolt rifle in .338 Lapua, 5.3 kg of steel and laminate that shrugs off the cold. 155 durability; the action is smooth as a bank vault. It is a rifle for a shot you get once, across a valley, through weather. Worth 340, and whoever owns it keeps the ammunition in a locked box and counts every round.

Bullpup precision rifle in .338 Lapua, 5.9 kg with the barrel mounted directly into the receiver for a straight line of recoil. 160 durability; the two-stage trigger and the scope mounts are machine-shop art. The bullpup layout keeps a full-length barrel inside a short overall length, which is the difference between a ridge shot and a hallway shot. Worth 380; it is the most expensive thing most bunkers own.

A 14 kg bolt-action rifle in .408 CheyTac, a caliber that barely exists and therefore travels farther than anything that does. 170 durability; the barrel is long, fluted, and free-floated, and the stock folds around the action like luggage. It is a rifle for a shot measured in kilometers, carried by a person who is paid in supplies. Worth 450, and its ammunition is counted in individual rounds.

Bolt-action long-range rifle in .408 CheyTac at 11.5 kg, lighter than its peers and still built like a bridge girder. 165 durability; the action is simple, which is what keeps it working when nobody can manufacture parts. One round, one shot, measured in kilometers. Worth 430, and the owner carries the cartridge in a padded case like a medical instrument.

Successor to the MK-X3 in the same .408 CheyTac, 12 kg with a refined action that still holds the tolerance of a gauge block. 165 durability; every part is machined and nothing is stamped. It is a rifle for the one shot that has to end the argument. Worth 440, and it usually changes hands with a target card from before the exchange taped to the case.

Semi-automatic anti-material rifle in .50 BMG, 14 kg of recoil-operated authority that flattens walls and stops engines. 180 durability; the muzzle brake throws most of the kick sideways, and the action has cycled a thousand rounds without complaint. It is a gun for a hole in a hillside, for a road nobody else can use. Worth 500, the ceiling of the arms trade here, and it is bought with things no one prices anymore.

Replaceable ballast for a UV grow lamp, 2.5 kg of coils and capacitors wrapped in tar. At 100 durability it is serviceable as long as it was stored dry. It powers lamps that keep greens alive through nuclear winter, and a lit shelf of them is a small green room in the gray. Worth 45; bunker managers buy spares before they buy food. The morale effect is three points of light in a place that has no windows.

A pressurized cylinder of refrigerant, 4 kg of the stuff that kept refrigerators cold before the exchange. It has no taste and no use on its own, but it is the blood of the last working cold-storage rooms, and those rooms hold the year's medicine and meat. At 100 durability the cylinder is sealed and trustworthy. Worth 60 in a region where spoiled insulin is a death sentence, and it empties fast.

A strip of dark glass wrapped in tape with slits cut for the eyes, 0.2 kg and built in an afternoon. The 60 durability means they last a season of glare at best, then get rebuilt. They keep the white winter light from burning out a scavenger's vision, which is the difference between walking home and being led home. Worth 12, and the first pair is never the last pair.

A small tube of grey thermal compound, 0.1 kg, enough to seat a dozen heatsinks. The 100 durability is only true if the seal holds; a cracked tube is a brick. It keeps the last CPUs and radios from overheating, and without it the scavenged electronics die one hot afternoon at a time. Worth 15, and radio operators hoard it in their kits like it is medicine, because it is.

A chunk of black ice chipped from a puddle that never fully froze clean, 1 kg, carried in a sealed bag. It carries a contamination of 0.85, which is why the bag has a biohazard stripe. It is not drinking water and it is not science, it is proof, carried from one hand to another, and everyone who carries it washes their hands twice. It weighs on the carrier the way the reading does.

A 5 kg steel canister, sealed and painted with a cobalt symbol, packed with salt that makes a counter stutter. Contamination at 0.95; the shielding is what makes it safe to transport, and the canister is EMP-shielded, so the latch still works when everything else is dead. Handling it costs health and morale, and no one carries it who does not have to. It is a question in a box, and the answer is not good.

A steel sled with a hand crank that drives a small wheel, 15 kg of honest labor saved on flat snow. The 150 durability means it survives winters that kill engines. It pulls what a person cannot carry: firewood, water, a body, if it comes to that. Worth 35, and after the first storm every household with one knows why the price is that low and the value is that high.

A tin of yellow salve, 0.2 kg, made from rendered fat and whatever numbs. Applied warm, it brings feeling back to white fingertips and buys back health worth of tissue that would otherwise be lost. The smell is strong and the relief is real. Worth 25, and the recipe is jealously guarded by whoever makes it, because winter makes everyone need it.

An 8 kg brass and steel valve built to survive a century of steam. The 300 durability is the highest rating on anything in common trade; it is a part for the deep geothermal line that heats the bunker, and when it seats, the whole wall warms. Worth 120, and it is one of the few things you can buy that pays for itself every winter. The morale lift is the heat coming back.

A 1.5 kg cartridge of soda-lime granules for the shelter scrubber. At 80 durability it is nearing the end of its service, and everyone in the bunker knows what a spent cartridge means: dull headaches, slow decisions, shorter tempers. When the new one seats, the air tastes clean again, and people sleep. Worth 40, and it is one of the few purchases that buys everyone a better night.

Rough-sawn 8 kg timbers, cut and squared by hand, kept dry and straight. They are the difference between a tunnel that stays up and a tunnel that comes down on someone. The bark is still on two faces, which means they were cut recently, which means there are still working sawmills somewhere. Worth 15 a length, cheap until the day the ceiling cracks and none are left.

4 kg bricks grown, not fired: fungus root packed into a mold and left to bind. They insulate better than concrete, weigh less, and cost 8, which makes them the cheapest building material a bunker can add. They are not load-bearing and everyone learns that once. The mold smell fades after a season, and the bricks keep growing back where they were patched.

A 1 kg cartridge of caustic granules that recycles a diver's or miner's air. At 40 durability it is already half spent, and a tired scrubber burns the throat on the second breath. It buys time in sealed rooms and flooded tunnels where there is no second air supply. Worth 35, and every canister sold comes with a promise about the last one that nobody repeats.

A 0.5 kg vial of black water, thick as oil, sealed with wax. It reads 0.8 contamination, and it takes 10 health to handle it without gloves, which everyone does once. It is not a sample of something, it is evidence of how bad the water table has become. The vial sits in a pack like a live coal, and the people who ask for it do not explain why.

A 1.5 kg reel of braided line with a clip at the end, for lowering a geiger counter into places a person should not go. You take the reading from above, from the length of the line. It is worth 20 and it is the cheapest life insurance in the wasteland, because the alternative is going down yourself with the counter in your hand. The line comes back smelling of dust.

A tuft of moss, 0.2 kg, that glows faint green in the dark, grown in a jar on a damp windowsill. It asks for nothing but shade and moisture, and it gives back 3 points of light where there is no electricity. Children touch it and adults stop and look. Worth 12, and the trader who grows it never sells the whole jar.

A 12 kg steel jack that lifts on compressed air, the kind that raises a truck or a fallen beam or a stuck hatch. It is worth 85 because it converts a two-day dig into an hour. It needs a compressor or a tank to run, and it needs a seal, and when the seal goes, the jack becomes a 12 kg paperweight. Everyone who owns one knows how to find the leak.

A 3 kg roll of reverse-osmosis membrane, the heart of the water purifier. At 100 durability it is still usable, and it will turn brackish, gritty water into something a child can drink. The membrane is the part that cannot be improvised, which is why it trades at 60 and why it is stolen from pumps when nobody is watching. It unrolls like a promise in a clean room.

A 2 kg tank and nozzle that turns fungicide into a fog that finds every corner of a damp room. The mold in bunkers eats cloth, lung, and morale, and the fog settles where hands cannot reach. Worth 45, and after a fogging the air is bitter for a day and the walls stay dry for a month. The smell of it means somebody is winning.

A 5 kg server blade pulled from a flooded basement, still bolted to its rails, corrosion blooming on the case. It has no power and no purpose until someone patient dries it, strips it, and reads what is on it. Worth 90 as data, not hardware. The last person who carried one out of a flood said the water was cold and the drive was warm, which made no sense and was true.

A 1.5 kg pole, jointed and spring-loaded, for tapping the ground ahead at arm's length. It is the tool that finds buried things before your foot does. Worth 15, and the people who use it tap in a rhythm that carries, and the people who hear the rhythm stop and wait. It is a poor tool for farming and the best tool for walking where others have walked.

3 kg of fine copper mesh, woven tight enough to block the pulse that kills electronics. A room lined with it keeps radios alive while everything outside goes dark and silent. Worth 45 a roll, and after the last EMP, the price tripled and never came back down. The mesh is also the best grounding for antennas, and it is never wasted.

A 2 kg box of batteries and a speaker that plays a loop of a generator, a gate, or a conversation, whatever you need a listener to hear. It draws attention the way a lit window does, and it is worth 30 for the time it buys. The loop ends and starts again with a click that no one notices except the person hiding nearby. It runs until the batteries die, which is the point.

A 0.8 kg circuit board, pulled from something that no longer exists, with the traces intact. It is worth 60 because somewhere a radio, a pump, or a charging station is missing exactly this board, and there are no new ones. The person who needs it will pay anything. It is carried wrapped in cloth, treated like a photograph of the dead: not useful to everyone, priceless to one.

4 kg of heavy panels, foam and quilted cloth, that swallow the sound of a room. A bunker lined with it can hold a conversation without the walls carrying it, and can run a generator without announcing the address. Worth 25, and the quiet it buys is worth more than the material. It is one of the few comforts that is also a defense.

A 1 kg canister with a fuse and an antenna coil that empties its charge through the air in a fraction of a second. Anything with a circuit within its reach goes dark: radios, pumps, and the other side's optics. It is worth 85 because it is the only weapon that wins a fight without firing a shot, and because the silence it leaves is total. The battery inside is the expensive part.

A 2.5 kg slug of tungsten, dense and grey, salvaged from a machine tool or a warhead. It is worth 40 because it is the weight that makes a penetrating round or a counterweight, and it cannot be forged from scrap. It takes a drill and patience to work. Every core in the region came out of something that no longer functions, and it will outlast the thing it goes into next.

A 1.2 kg coil of reinforced hose, the artery for any air tool or jack. It is worth 18 and it is the part that fails first, the one people forget until the compressor is running and the tool is dead. A good length is kept coiled, ends capped against dirt, because dirt is what kills it. The repair shops trade it in meters, and nobody argues the price.

A 0.5 kg key on a worn lanyard, stamped with a number and no owner's name. It opens doors that were meant to stay shut, the override for a system whose makers are gone. There is no price for it because no one will sell it, only pass it along with instructions that are shorter than the consequences. It is carried close, and it is never shown.

A 0.4 kg set of over-ear headphones, the heavy kind from a radio room, with the padding gone flat. They still isolate sound, which is worth 22 to anyone listening for a generator, a footstep, or a signal through static. The cord has been replaced twice. The people who wear them look at the world a half-second late and hear everything first.

A 3 kg gun built for two-part epoxy, with the mixing nozzle that pays for itself. At 100 durability it is a working tool, and it will seal a hull seam, fix a pipe, or hold a crack in the shelter wall for another winter. Worth 65, and the cartridges cost as much as the gun. It is the tool of people who repair instead of replace, because there is no replace.

6 kg lengths of galvanized rebar, the zinc coating still holding against rust. It is worth 25 a length because it is the skeleton of everything rebuilt: concrete, gates, and the frames of greenhouses that keep food alive. The coating means it lasts years where bare steel would flake in a season. Salvage crews cut it from old foundations, and every length has a past.

A 2.5 kg visor with lead sheet laminated into the shell, worn for work in hot zones. It gives 15 rad protection against the dose that comes through the face, and the tinted glass cuts the glare of ash fields. At 100 durability it is sound, and the EMP shielding means the face protection is not held together by electronics. Worth 80; it is the difference between looking at the world and being burned by it.

A 0.5 kg pane of dark glass that blocks the flash that blinds. It is worth 35 because welders are the ones who keep everything else working, and a welder without glass is a welder with one eye. The pane slides into any helmet and outlasts the helmet. Salvage crews fight over intact panes before they fight over the torches, because the torch is replaceable and the eye is not.

A dried root, 0.2 kg, that the old herbalists chewed for motion sickness and fear. The dose is thin and the cost is real: it takes 5 health to use it, and the taste is a punishment. It is worth 45 because it is one of the few things left that works when the pharmacy shelves are bare. Traders keep it in a tin with a mark drawn on the lid.

A 0.5 kg jar of white salt, measured in pinches, that steadies a mind that has been grinding too long. It costs 10 thirst for every dose, and it is worth it to people who have stopped sleeping. It buys 15 points of steadiness at the price of a canteen. Worth 50, and the jar is passed around carefully, because the line between steady and dull is a pinch.

A 0.8 kg shard of mirror, edges taped, the silver still bright on the back. It is worth 10, and it is the cheapest signal anyone can own: flash, aim, or just look at your own face once a week to remember what it is. It works where batteries do not. The shards come from furniture and dressing tables, and they catch light the way the old world did.

A 0.3 kg disc of polished aluminum from a sealed drive, the data layer intact, carried in an EMP-shielded case. It is the only kind of memory that survived the pulse, and the machines to read it are rare and guarded. It is worth nothing in trade and everything to the person who knows what is on it. It catches light like a mirror and holds a secret like a vault.

A 1.5 kg harness of webbing and steel clips, worn over a coat, with a ring that takes a rope or a safety line. At 100 durability it is still sound, and the buckles are the kind that hold no matter how much you shake. It is for roofs, shafts, and ice, the places where a slip is the end. Worth 20, and the people who wear it check the stitching every morning.

A 1 kg sheet of plastic grown from fermented starch, pressed and cured into boards and fittings. It is worth 15, cheaper than anything from a factory, and it is the material of the second world: compostable, repairable, and good enough for pipes, panels, and crates. It degrades in sunlight, so it is stored in the dark. The smell of it is the smell of a workshop that still works.

A 0.4 kg bottle of dark syrup that makes a memory go soft at the edges. It costs 5 health, and it is worth 40 to anyone who has seen what the first days of the exchange looked like. It does not erase, it blurs, and a blurred memory is easier to carry. The traders do not ask what for, and the buyers do not say. The bottle is measured in sips, not doses.

A 0.3 kg cassette in a cracked case, the label hand-written. It is worth 30 and it gives 10 points of something that ration cards never will: a voice, a song, a game broadcast, the sound of before. The players that still work are kept in bunkers like organs. The tape is traded on trust, because nobody rewinds it before they sell it, and nobody has to.

A 0.5 kg album with a cloth cover, filled with photographs of people standing in front of houses that no longer exist. It is worth 40 and it is the strongest single thing of its kind: 15 points of proof that the world was warm and ordinary. It is passed around a bunker on quiet nights, and the pages are turned slowly. Nobody writes names in it anymore, because the names are gone.

2 kg of records in paper sleeves, stacked in a milk crate, the edges worn from a hundred hands. It is worth 50 and it lifts morale 20 points when the needle drops, the loudest, warmest thing in any bunker. The turntables that survive are fewer each year, and the records are priced by condition, not song. Every collection has one cracked record that nobody throws away.

A 3 kg coverall stitched with ash-grey shreds until it looks like a patch of burned ground. It gives 20 rad protection by keeping fallout off the cloth and skin beneath, and it hides a prone body at ten meters. At 100 durability it is still intact, which is rare, because the suit is dragged through everything. Worth 70; it is the difference between being seen and being walked past.

A 0.4 kg ring of cured rubber, the size of a dinner plate, still supple. It is worth 8 and it is the cheapest seal that keeps water out and air in, the part that fails in a cold snap and costs a room. It is the kind of thing bought in fours, because one is never enough. The rubber was cured before the exchange, and it will outlast the machine it was made for.

A 2.5 kg bag of dry mix, cement and sand measured out by hand, tied at the neck. It is worth 6 and it is the mortar of small repairs: cracks, steps, and the corner of a wall that drips. One bag is a morning's work and a patch that will outlast the person who mixes it. The bags are hoarded in dry corners, and the dry corners are the first thing checked after a leak.

A 0.2 kg roll of black tape, sticky on one side and patient on the other. It is worth 4 and it is the first thing in every repair kit: wiring, handles, hoses, and the cracks in a mask strap at 3 am. It is not a real fix, and everyone who uses it knows that, and it still holds until the real fix exists. The roll is the last thing a room runs out of.

A 60 kg engine block, complete, the deck flat and the bores still round. It is worth 120 because it is the difference between a truck and a shed full of parts, and because nobody can cast one new. It takes four people and a ramp to move it, and every workshop has a corner worn smooth by the last one that sat there. It is bought by people who intend to finish the job.

A 1.5 kg boxed set of industrial bearings, still in their grease paper, the sizes written on the lid. They are worth 18 and they are what keeps a shaft turning when the whole region has stopped: pumps, wheels, winches. Clean bearings are the difference between a machine and a monument. The set is checked and re-greased once a month, and the paper is saved.

A 1.8 kg length of copper tubing, capped at both ends, a meter of the metal that plumbing and power both run on. It is worth 9, and it is traded in full lengths because a cut end is a wasted end. The caps mean it was stored against dirt and kinks. Every length is a repair waiting to happen, and repair is the industry of the third year.

A few pages of paper, 0.05 kg, printed on the last working copier, with the building's name stamped on every page. It lists cracks, sags, and the room that should not be used. It is a document with no price, only a routing: from the engineer's desk to the people who have to live with the findings. The corners are folded from being carried. Nobody reads it aloud to the children.

A 4 kg bag of dry concrete mix, cement, sand, and gravel in the right proportions, tied shut against the damp. It is worth 6, and it is the material of permanence in a world of patched things: foundations, walls, and the base of a stove that will be there after the stove is gone. One bag makes one small pour. The measure is a coffee can, and everyone has one.

A 3.5 kg length of steel rebar, the ribs still sharp, the cut ends rusted where the saw bit. It is worth 7, and it is the spine of every pour and every gate, the thing that keeps concrete honest when it cracks. It is carried on a shoulder like a walking stick, and it is never wasted: even the cut ends become stakes and hooks. The salvage comes from bones of buildings.

A page of transcribed radio traffic, 0.05 kg, logged on 142.5 MHz, the frequency people still trust. It is written in the cramped hand of whoever was on watch, with times, callsigns, and the gaps where the signal dropped. It is a document with no price, but it is worth reading twice, because the second read is where the pattern sits. The page is coffee-ringed and smudged, and the last line is unfinished.

A 0.6 kg coil of enameled wire, wound tight, the kind that tunes an antenna to a voice in the static. It is worth 8 and it is the difference between a dead radio and a live one, between calling out and shouting at nothing. The coil is counted in meters and the enamel is checked for nicks, because a nick is silence. Every radio room keeps a spare on a nail above the bench.

A 0.05 kg page of bearings, times, and crossed lines drawn with a ruler, fixing a signal to a point on a map. It is the work of three listening posts and a cold night of math. It has no price and it names no names, only coordinates. The pencil marks are soft, erased and redrawn. Someone folded it into a coat pocket and walked toward the point, and the page does not say how that walk ended.

A 0.05 kg form, carbon-smeared, with boxes for temperature, dose, and symptoms, and a line for the interviewer's note. It is the paperwork of mercy and suspicion at once, the gate every traveler passes through. The handwriting changes on every line because the desk rotates. The last box is for a decision, and the decisions are not recorded anywhere else. The form is filed, and the filing cabinet is the whole story.

A 0.05 kg ledger page, ruled and dated, listing stores by category: food, fuel, medicine, and the column for things that ran out. The numbers are in pencil, the crossings-out in pen, because corrections are permanent and mistakes are not. It is the most honest document a bunker produces, and the most feared, because it cannot be argued with. The bottom line is added once a month, and nobody likes the total.

A 0.05 kg medical form with a diagnosis written in one line: acute radiation syndrome, and the stage. The rest of the page is labs and vitals and the space for a name that is sometimes left blank. It is paperwork that becomes a calendar, counting days. It has no price and it is carried like a stone. The doctor's signature is the same on every copy, and the prognosis is not on the page, but everyone reads it there.

A 0.05 kg inventory sheet for the medical locker: dressings, antibiotics, the painkillers kept under lock, and the column for expired stock. The counts are honest because the person who counts is the person who will need them. It is worth nothing and it decides everything: who gets treated, who gets rationed, who gets a blanket instead. The sheet is updated after every emergency, and the pen lives on a string.

A 0.05 kg protocol sheet, laminated and dog-eared, listing the steps for a case no doctor wants: what to give, what to hold, and when to stop. It is typed by a committee that is gone, and followed by people who never met them. The margins carry hand-written notes from two winters of use. It is not a cure, it is a procedure, and in the wasteland a procedure is the closest thing to hope that can be written down.

A 1.2 kg coil of copper wiring, the insulation cracking in places, the conductor bright where it is stripped. It is worth 7 and it is the nervous system of everything rebuilt: lights, radios, and the pump that keeps water moving. It is traded by weight, and the scrap buyers are always watching the price. A good coil is hidden from thieves and measured out in lengths, because every meter is a circuit.

A 0.05 kg inspection sheet for the shelter air intake, dated and signed, with a diagram of the valve and a grease mark where the inspector's thumb rested. It lists the seal condition, the filter state, and the torque on the bolts. It is the paperwork of staying alive without thinking about it. The next inspection date is written at the top in a different hand, and the date is sooner than last time.

A 0.1 kg vial of cloudy water, sealed with a numbered tag and a wax cap. It was taken from a source people used to trust, and the number on the tag is the reading everyone is waiting for. It is evidence, and evidence has a weight that the scales do not show. The vial sits in a padded case, and the case sits in a backpack, and the backpack is carried like a verdict.

A 0.1 kg roll of blueprints, held by a rubber band that is older than the plans. It is worth 2, and it is worth 5 morale to the person who reads it with a lamp, because the plans are for something that will exist again: a well, a workshop, a better room. The paper is thin and the lines are sure. It is a document about the future, and that alone is rare enough to trade.

A 0.3 kg headset with the foam gone and the band taped, the wire spliced twice. It is worth 2, and it is worth 5 morale to the person who puts it on, because it still carries a voice from somewhere else, and somewhere else still exists. The static is louder than the signal now, and the listener keeps the volume low to save the batteries. It is worn like a habit, and it works like one.

A 0.9 kg service pistol, blued steel worn to grey, holstered on a belt that no longer has a uniform on it. It is worth 2 and it is worth 5 morale to the hand that knows its weight, because it is proof that the owner was once issued a role and a place. The safety is checked with a thumb, from muscle memory. It is not fired much, and no one asks why it is kept.

A 0.02 kg surgical mask, folded flat, the paper creased and yellowed, the ear loops still elastic. It is worth 2, and it is worth 5 morale to the person who keeps it, because it came from a hospital that used to be a place of help. It is not worn; it is kept, in a pocket, against the day when the last one wears out. It is the smallest thing anyone saves, and the reason is the same as the biggest.

Vacuum-sealed ration blocks, dense and shelf-stable. Chewing them is a chore and they taste of cardboard and salt, but they keep for years and pack small. The label says they were made for "continuity of operations", which is what the Office calls not starving.
A sealed power cell from before the exchange, still holding a charge. They are heavy, they are quiet, and everyone wants them: lamps, radios, pumps, the machines that make life indoors possible.
A foil emergency blanket, still folded tight in its pouch. It traps body heat without weight, which matters in a corridor where the frost creeps under every door.
A bottle of clear spirits, distilled from something that grew in the wasteland. It burns going down and warms the chest, and in the long dark that warmth is worth something.
A dented can of condensed soup, label peeled half off. The contents are grey but honest. Heat it or eat it cold; it is calories either way.
A bundle of rechargeable cells wired into a carry pack, the kind that kept a radio running through a bad night. Every amp is spoken for in this shelter.
A military-grade encrypted storage drive, intact. The data on it survived the exchange; the passphrase did not. Someone somewhere would pay to read what it holds.
A pot of stencil ink for marking crates and manifests. The Overlay keeps records in triplicate; the ink keeps them readable.
A box of 5.56mm rounds, sealed against the damp. Firearms still work if the ammunition is dry, and dry ammunition is worth more than the rifle.
A box of .308 rounds, brass cases tarnished but serviceable. One good rifle shot is a statement; a box of these is a position.
A sealed box of 7.62mm rounds. Military-issue, crimped primers, no corrosion. The garrison would trade well for these.
A military meal, still in its shrink wrap. Main dish, side, cracker, powder drink, a spoon. Years old and better preserved than anything the shelves hold now.
Sealed ration packs from a supply cache. Boring, salty, and exactly the calories the label promises.
A compact surgical kit in a canvas roll: scalpel, forceps, sutures, a small vial of antiseptic. Made for tents and field stations, built to be used fast.
A sealed strip of potassium iodide tablets. They protect the thyroid from absorbing fallout, which is not nothing, though it is not everything either.
A tube of purification tablets. Drop one in a canteen and wait twenty minutes. The water tastes of chlorine and certainty.
A five-litre jug of clean water, sealed and heavy. Real water, no colour, no grit, no questions at the bottom of the glass.
A small stack of children's books, covers worn soft. In the bunker they are read until they fall apart, because they are the only place where things work out.
A pack of AA batteries. Small, scarce, and endlessly demanded: the clocks, the radios, the torches, the hearing aids all run on them.
Paper packets of vegetable seeds, printed instructions still legible. In the right soil and the right light they become food; in the wrong hands they become hope.
A field radio in a battered transit case. It still receives; transmitting is a question of power, antenna, and nerve.
A night vision scope with a cracked objective lens but a working intensifier tube. It turns the black outside into a grey world of shapes.
A cloth bag lined with copper mesh. Electronics inside survive an electromagnetic pulse; everything else in the wasteland does not.
A sealed drum of diesel, sloshing heavy. Engines, generators, pumps: the wasteland runs on it until the day it stops running.
A pre-war manual on greenhouse cultivation, spine cracked at the page on root vegetables. The theory survives; the seasons no longer do.
A small bottle of lens cleaner and a soft cloth. For a camera that survived the exchange, it is worth more than gold.
A box of photographic film, kept dry. Somewhere there is a camera that still works, and film is the only way to make the wasteland remember.
The metal comb from a music box, teeth intact. It is the part that makes the notes; without it the cylinder only turns.
A small hand-cranked music box that plays Für Elise. Wind it and the tune survives, fragile and absurd, into a world that forgot music.
A winding key for a clockwork device. Small, precise, and useless until it is the only thing standing between you and silence.
A tin of light machine oil. Every hinge, every bearing, every door in the shelter asks for it eventually.
A can of heavy machine oil for moving parts under load. Generators, pumps, lathes: metal needs feeding too.
A box of gears, bearings, springs, and fasteners sorted by size. The raw vocabulary of repair.
A handful of brass fittings, valves and connectors. Brass does not rust, which makes it the currency of anyone who fixes pipes.
A locket containing a faded photograph of a family. It survived; they may not have. Some things carry weight beyond their grams.
A small padded coat, cut for a child, with a hood and a face flap. It was made to keep someone small warm and covered.
A spool of typewriter ribbon, still in its box. The machine that takes it is heavy, loud, and one of the few ways the record gets kept.
A worn leather pouch of dried tobacco. In the bunker it is not a habit; it is a social compact, passed hand to hand.
A sealed military supply crate, stencilled with a unit mark that means nothing now. What it holds decides what it is worth.

A laminated rank chit, Iron Garrison issue, the photo bleached to a grey oval but the embossed name still legible under a thumb run sideways across it: VOSS, T. COL. The reverse carries a call-sign stamp, LIMA-NOVEMBER-SEVEN-FOUR, the ink gone rust-brown. Command records this chit as destroyed with its owner. It was not. Whoever carried it last kept it dry, kept it flat, and did not sell it, which in this district is the closest thing to a character reference an object can offer.

Half a bulletin, ripped along a fold that has been folded and unfolded too many times to hold ink evenly. What survives reads Reclamation is not repudiation and stops there, the rest lost to a burn hole the shape of a dropped cigarette. Somebody wanted to keep this half badly enough to carry it. The other half, if it exists, would say what Colonel Harven actually meant by that sentence, and three years on nobody has produced it.

A brass counterweight, one kilo exactly, its stamped number worn to a suggestion by three years of hands setting it on the pan and taking it off again. The Grain Exchange owns eleven of these and can account for all eleven at any hour of any day, which is either the most impressive thing about the place or the only thing keeping it standing, depending on which trader you ask after a bad harvest.

A meter of reflective tape, D/9 doctrine orange, cut in the specific length and tied at the specific height their manual requires for a marked charge. It came off Railway Span 44-Alpha, which means someone either disarmed a live demolition lead or is lying about where they found this, and there is no polite way to ask which.

A T-handled key, forged not machined, that opens the main irrigation valve at the Terrace Pumphouse. Three copies were ever made. This district has fought two documented wars over a fourth copy that may not exist. Whoever is holding this key controls whether the south slope drinks this season, which is a great deal of authority to hang from a loop of baling wire.

A page torn from a fixer's account book, columns headed in a cramped, cheerful hand: OWES ME, OWES ME MORE, WILL OWE ME. Under the third column, someone has written the Central Garrison's requisition officer, the Grain Exchange's head weigher, and a name crossed out so hard the pencil tore the paper. Barrow Fennick has never once, in three years, been on the wrong side of a debt when the shooting started. People find this more suspicious than reassuring.

The wooden handle of a queue-line paint stick, the bristle end burned to a black stub. The plaza's lines were repainted every few weeks for three years running, cheaper than riot control and just as effective. This one was mid-stroke on a fresh line when the strike came. The line it was painting is still visible in the crater's ash shadow, half a stroke long, pointing at nothing in particular now.

A page from a one-time authentication pad, most of its rows already used and crossed through in a steady hand. The header block reads LIMA-NOVEMBER-SEVEN-FOUR, retired from active service the same week Colonel Voss did. Whoever is still burning through these rows either kept a spare pad for three years out of sentiment, or never stopped being issued them, and the second possibility is the one nobody in the Garrison wants to say out loud.

A pilgrim's personal dosimeter, cheap stamped casing, worn on a cord gone soft with sweat. The reading is lower than it has any right to be for ground this close to six months of shelling, and the Ash Sign preachers hold it up as the clearest proof yet that the fire spares its own. A careful person might instead ask who else has been near this exact stretch of ground recently, and why, and get no useful answer either way.

A carbon receipt from the Weighbridge, the rate line struck through twice and rewritten twice higher, both times in the Tollman's own hand, both times without an explanation offered or asked for. The war has been very good business for the one crossing that never closes. Someone has scrawled a third figure in the margin, unofficial, in pencil: what it would cost if you needed to cross tonight, no questions, and did not want the Tollman to remember your face.

A stamped metal ration token, standard issue, except a child has scratched a small five-pointed star into the face with something sharp and colored it in with chalk dust rubbed into the scratches. It still spends at full value at the Exchange. Whoever finds it usually spends it on something else instead and keeps the token, which is not what the district's food economy needs right now and is exactly what the district needs right now, depending on how the day has gone.

A strip of Exchange trade cloth, the same bolt used for the trestle-table awnings, tied around an upper arm with a plain overhand knot. No insignia, no unit name stitched on, because the twelve who first tied one on couldn't agree what to call themselves and the argument is still open. Everyone in the district recognizes the cloth anyway. It has come to mean something whether or not anyone chose it to.

A single page from a demolition cache inventory, ruled columns filled in a draftsman's hand: charge count, detonator count, condition, last verified. The last verified date is recent — inside the season, not inside the war. Whoever maintains this cache is still counting, still ruling neat columns, four years after the last order that could plausibly have asked them to. The page doesn't explain why. Doctrine doesn't require it to.

A scrap of cloth tied to the waystation lean-to, sun-bleached past whatever color it started, with a number inked on it in a hand too faded to read. Pilgrims tie one on the way up and untie it on the way down, or don't, depending on what the shrine told them. The lean-to post has more knots in its wood than cloth left flying, which either means the wind is hard on flags or the walk down changes people's minds more than the walk up.

A hand-wound induction coil, spare, still in its wax-paper wrapping, the kind of part that keeps a low-power relay broadcasting after the factory-made ones burn out one by one. Whoever wound this knew exactly what they were building it for and never signed their work, which tracks: nothing about The Understory's relay chain has ever had a name attached to it, and everyone involved seems to prefer it stays that way.

A brass hand-stamp, the Continuity Office's seal cut into its face, worn smooth at the edges from three years of pressing wax and ink alike. Every decree that has gone up at Checkpoint Gamma since Day 238 carries this exact impression, meaning whoever holds it can make a bulletin official with one press of a hand. The Office would very much like it back. The Office has not offered to say why it went missing in the first place.

Half a page of meeting minutes in a steady, economical hand: motion carried, four to one, and the numbers of who voted which way, though the names have been abbreviated to initials in a way that reads like habit rather than secrecy. The torn edge cuts off mid-sentence, right where the minutes were about to record what the vote was actually about. Adaeze Okonkwo's roster writes everything down. Not everyone who finds a page of it gets to keep reading.

A trail lantern, the glass cracked and taped rather than replaced, carried up and down the switchback so often the handle's leather wrap has worn through to the wire beneath. Toma Reyes has climbed to the shrine and back by this lantern's light more nights than she's kept count of, by her own admission, which for a woman who otherwise measures everything in numbers is itself worth noting.

A card filing tag, string loop still attached, the kind clipped to a folder in an archive that expected to still be an archive in a year's time. Stamped in the corner: LOGGED, NOT CHASED — R.RUHL. Whoever Ruhl was, they had a whole system for the things this district couldn't explain, one tag per unexplained thing, filed and left. This is one tag out of what was clearly meant to be many. Nobody has found the rest of the drawer.

A torn corner of the schedule chalked on the watch container's door, four names to a shift, two of the four crossed through and rewritten in a different hand's slant. Whoever keeps the roster still lays it out the way the Rebuilders taught them — start time, relief time, sidearm check, initials — three years of drilled habit outlasting the argument that split them off. Nobody has corrected the format. Nobody has needed to.

A second page, stapled behind a cache manifest, this one a denial-priority list rather than an inventory: targets ranked by how much damage leaving them standing would do if the wrong hands took them. A line reading FORWARD (TOLL, SPLINTER, EX-REBUILDER) has been added at the bottom in one hand, bracketed with a question mark in a second, then underlined twice in the first hand again, as if the argument kept going after the pen changed direction. No verdict is written down. Denial lists don't usually leave room for one.

A page from the shrine liturgy, hand-copied like all the others, except this one has a line struck through — the ground remembers where not to fall — and nothing written in its place. Every shrine-keeper before this year could recite that line without thinking about it. Since the crater opened at the cairn's foot, nobody has tried. The blank space under the strikethrough has been left blank for weeks now, which the pilgrims have started reading as its own kind of verse.

A page torn from the log taped inside a stairwell door, nothing on it but call times, no names, no station markers, set down in at least three different sets of handwriting. The times don't follow a fixed schedule, which is deliberate — a moving broadcast is a broadcast nobody can silence by knowing where to point. Whoever tore this page loose either needed proof the relay had been active on a given night, or needed to make sure nobody else could use it as exactly that.
